title: As a developer, I can create a feature flag and toggle it live in production within minutes of signing up
As a developer, I can target flags with attribute-based rules and reusable segments so the right users see the right variation
As a developer, I can target or exclude specific individual users for a flag (allowlists, beta testers, internal accounts)
As a developer, I can serve multivariate flags and dynamic configuration values (strings, numbers, JSON), not just booleans
As a developer, I can manage separate environments (dev/staging/prod) with independent flag states and scoped SDK keys
As a platform engineer, I can find stale flags and code references so temporary flags actually get removed from the codebase
As a developer, I can roll a flag out progressively by percentage with consistent bucketing, ramping from 1% to 100% without redeploying
As a platform engineer, I can guard a rollout with metrics so a regression is detected and the release is rolled back automatically
As a developer, I can schedule flag changes and releases to happen at a specific future time
As a product manager, I can run A/B and multivariate experiments on flags and see which variation wins on my metrics
As a product manager, I can trust a documented statistics engine (Bayesian or frequentist, with variance-reduction options) behind experiment results
As a product manager, I can define experiment metrics from my own data — warehouse tables or ingested events — instead of a black-box metric store
As an AI agent, I can read experiment configurations and results programmatically to summarize outcomes and recommend ship/rollback decisions
As a developer, I can use official SDKs across my whole stack — backend, web, and mobile — with consistent flag behavior
As a platform engineer, my server SDKs evaluate flags locally from a cached ruleset — microsecond decisions with no network call per flag check
As a platform engineer, I can evaluate flags at the edge (CDN workers or an edge/relay layer) close to users
As a developer, flag changes propagate to connected SDKs in seconds via streaming or fast polling — a kill switch actually kills
As a platform engineer, I can use the vendor through OpenFeature providers so my flag code isn't locked to one vendor's SDK API
As a platform engineer, every flag change is recorded in an audit log — who changed what, when, and to which value
As a platform engineer, I can require approvals or change requests before production flag changes go live
As a platform engineer, I can restrict who can change which flags with roles, permissions, and scoped API tokens

As an AI agent, I can create and toggle flags through documented APIs, CLIs, or MCP — and the platform can force my changes through approval workflows instead of letting me write to production unreviewed
As a platform engineer, I can self-host the full flag platform from an open-source distribution, keeping evaluation data on my infrastructure
As a platform engineer, I can run a relay/edge proxy so flags stay served when the vendor is unreachable and SDK traffic stays inside my network
As a product manager, I can see published pricing and understand what drives cost (seats, MAUs, events, requests) before committing
